intro.title: Functional requirements
script: Before drawing anything, I want to agree on **what Dropbox does** for this design. At its heart it's a **folder that lives in the cloud**: you drop a file in it on your laptop, and it shows up on your phone, on your other computers, and for anyone you've shared it with.

The product looks simple, and that's exactly what makes it hard: users expect it to **just work**, invisibly, for files of any size, on flaky networks, across devices that go offline for days. I'll scope it to the core of file sync and sharing.

cards.title: Upload & download
script: First, users can **upload and download files** of any type, from a tiny text file to a 50 GB video. Big files must survive a dropped connection halfway through without starting over.

cards.title: Folders & metadata
script: Second, files live in a **folder tree**. Users create folders and rename, move and delete files and folders. Notice that most of these operations touch **only metadata**: renaming a 10 GB folder shouldn't move a single byte of file content.

cards.title: Automatic sync
lines: changes reach other devices in seconds
script: Third, and this is the defining feature: **automatic sync**. A desktop client watches a local folder, notices every change, and pushes it up. Every other device the user owns picks the change up within a few seconds, without anyone pressing a button.

cards.title: Offline edits & conflicts
script: Fourth, devices go **offline**: a laptop on a plane keeps editing files. When it comes back online, we reconcile. If two devices changed the same file, we **never silently throw one edit away**; we keep both, and the loser becomes a *conflicted copy*.

cards.title: Version history
script: Fifth, **version history**. Users can see earlier versions of a file and restore any of them, and **deleted files** can be recovered for 30 days. That's both a feature and our safety net against ransomware and accidental deletes.

cards.title: Shared folders
lines: Share a folder with other users
script: Sixth, **shared folders**. A user shares a folder with teammates, as editors or viewers, and it appears in each member's own Dropbox, syncing to all of their devices. One edit has to fan out to everyone who can see it.

cards.title: Share links
script: And seventh, **share links**: a URL that lets anyone, even without an account, view or download a file or folder. These can go viral, so this is a read path that has to handle a sudden flood of strangers.

outOfScope.title: Out of scope
script: I'm leaving out **real-time co-editing** (that's Google Docs or Dropbox Paper, a different problem), **full-text search** and content indexing, **previews and thumbnails**, camera upload, billing and quotas, the team admin console, and **end-to-end encryption**, which would change the dedupe story a lot.
Some of these hang off the same change stream we'll build, so I'll point at where they'd plug in, but I won't design them.
lines: Real-time co-editing (Paper)  ·  Full-text search  ·  Previews & thumbnails  ·  Camera upload
Billing & quotas  ·  Admin console  ·  End-to-end encryption

intro.title: Non-functional requirements
script: Now the qualities. Two of them dominate everything else: we must **never lose a file**, and the system has to be **cheap enough to store exabytes**. Most of the design falls out of balancing those two.

cards.title: Scale
script: For **scale** I'll assume **500 million registered users**, about **100 million daily actives**, and around **20 file changes per active user per day**, so roughly **2 billion changes a day**.

cards.title: Sync latency
script: On **latency**: a small change should show up on the user's other devices in **under five seconds**. Metadata operations like listing a folder or renaming a file should be under **200 milliseconds at p99**. Uploading a big file is bandwidth-bound, so the goal there is throughput, not latency.

cards.title: Availability
script: **Availability**: four nines for the metadata and sync paths. And the client helps here: because it keeps a full local copy, a short outage just means sync pauses; the user can keep working in their folder and we catch up later.

cards.title: Durability
script: **Durability** is the non-negotiable one: **eleven nines**. Once we've told a client a file is saved, we must never lose it. People keep their tax returns and their baby photos here. Losing a file is the one failure users never forgive.

cards.title: Consistency
script: **Consistency**: within one folder tree, changes must be **strongly ordered**, so every device applies them in the same order and **converges on the same state**. A rename followed by an edit must never be replayed as an edit followed by a rename. Across unrelated users, we need no coordination at all.

cards.title: Bandwidth efficiency
lines: never upload the same bytes twice
script: **Bandwidth efficiency**: editing one slide in a 200 MB presentation must not re-upload 200 MB. We send **only what changed**, and we never upload bytes the server already has. This matters for user experience on slow links and for our own network bill.

cards.title: Cost
script: And **cost**. Storage is the dominant cost of the whole business; it's the line on the P&L that decides whether Dropbox is profitable. Every byte we store gets stored for years, so a 10% saving in storage overhead is worth a lot of engineering.

estimates.title: Back-of-the-envelope estimates
script: The numbers. **500 million users** storing an average of about **6 GB** each is roughly **3 exabytes** of logical data. Block-level dedupe saves about a quarter of that, and erasure coding adds about 40% overhead instead of the 200% that triple replication would, so we land around **3 exabytes on disk**.

**2 billion changes a day** is about **23,000 commits a second** on average, maybe **70,000** at peak. If each change uploads about a megabyte of new blocks, that's **2 petabytes a day** coming in, about 23 GB a second, and downloads are a few times that because every change goes to several devices.

On the metadata side: say **2,000 files per user**, so a trillion file entries at a few hundred bytes each, about **250 TB** before version history. And **100 million devices online** each holding a long-poll connection; with a 90-second poll timeout that's over **a million reconnects a second**.

takeaway.title: Takeaway: two very different problems
takeaway.heading: Takeaway: split the file bytes from the file tree
script: So the takeaway: Dropbox is really **two systems with opposite shapes**. The **file bytes** are exabytes of immutable data: we want them cheap, durable, deduplicated and easy to cache, and we don't need transactions over them at all.

The **file tree**, the metadata, is tiny by comparison, a few hundred terabytes, but it's where all the hard correctness lives: ordering, conflicts, sharing, permissions. The whole design is about **keeping those two apart** and giving each the storage it deserves.
lines: Bytes: ~3 EB, immutable → content-addressed blocks, dedupe, erasure coding, cold tiers
Tree: ~250 TB, ~25K commits/s, must be ordered → a sharded SQL journal per namespace

slides.title: Start simple: a client and one server
script: Let's start with the simplest thing that could work: a **desktop client** on the user's laptop, and **one server** of ours. When a file changes in the Dropbox folder, the client uploads the whole file; when the user opens it on another machine, that machine downloads it.

This already delivers the basic promise, a folder that lives in the cloud. But it has every problem we listed: the server is a single point of failure, there's nowhere durable to keep anything, and a one-byte edit to a 2 GB file re-uploads 2 GB. Everything we add from here fixes one of those problems.

slides.title: A database for the file tree
script: The first thing the server needs is somewhere to keep the **file tree**: which files exist, in which folders, with what size, modification time and version. That's classic relational data, so I'd put it in **MySQL**, with a files table keyed by user and path.

slides.title: Renames touch only rows
script: Getting the tree into its own store pays off right away for the folder operations. A **rename or a move is a metadata update**: we change a row, or a set of rows for a folder, and the file contents don't move at all. Listing a folder is an indexed query. Keep this split in mind, the tree on one side and the bytes on the other, because it's the backbone of the whole design.

slides.title: File bytes go in blob storage
script: The **file contents** definitely don't belong in MySQL. Exabytes of opaque bytes want an **object store**: something like S3, where we put and get blobs by key, and that's built for capacity and durability rather than queries.

slides.title: Bytes first, metadata second
script: So now an upload writes the bytes to blob storage and then a row in the database pointing at them. Notice the order: **bytes first, metadata second**.

slides.title: If we crash in between
script: If we crash in between, we've leaked some storage that a cleanup job can find later. Doing it the other way round would leave a row pointing at a file that doesn't exist, which is much worse.
We're still uploading and storing **whole files**, though. That's the next thing to fix.

rows: an orphan blob nobody points at
a little leaked storage; cleanup finds it
a broken file the user can see

slides.title: A load balancer and stateless servers
script: Before going further, let's deal with the **single server**. We put a **load balancer** in front, terminating TLS and authenticating each device's token, and run many identical copies of the server behind it.

That only works if the servers are **stateless**: everything they need lives in the database or the blob store, so any request can go to any server and we can add or drain servers freely. The load balancer will also become our router: as we split the server into specialized services, it sends each request to the right one by path, like a small API gateway.

slides.title: Split files into content-addressed blocks
script: Now the big idea. Instead of treating a file as one blob, the client **splits it into blocks of up to 4 MB** and computes a **SHA-256 hash** of each block. A file becomes simply an **ordered list of block hashes**.

slides.title: Content addressing
script: We store blocks in blob storage **keyed by their hash**. That's called **content addressing**, and it gives us a lot.

slides.title: What content addressing buys us
script: Blocks are **immutable**, because a block's name *is* its content, so we can cache them anywhere forever. A failed upload of a 10 GB file resumes from the last block, not from zero. Blocks upload in parallel. And when one byte changes, only the one block containing it gets a new hash.

items.detail: cache any block anywhere, forever

items.text: **Resumable**: a failed 10 GB upload restarts mid-way
items.detail: from the last block, not from zero
fills the pipe on fast links
one changed byte → one new block hash

slides.title: The Block Service: the data plane
script: The bytes now flow through a dedicated **Block Service** with a simple API: put a block, get a block. It's the data plane, and it scales on bandwidth, independently of everything else.

slides.title: The Metadata Service and the commit
script: What's left of the old server becomes the **Metadata Service**, the control plane. It owns the file tree and knows nothing about bytes.

slides.title: Saving a file is a commit
script: Saving a file is now a **commit**: the client sends "this path is now this list of block hashes", along with the version it last saw. The Metadata Service records the new version in a single transaction. A file version is just a row pointing at hashes, which makes versions almost free; we'll come back to that.

steps.label: BEGIN · INSERT v8 → [h1, h2, h3] · COMMIT

steps.note: a version is a row of hashes: almost free

slides.title: Two planes, two scaling axes
script: Separating the planes means each one scales on its own axis: the Block Service on **bandwidth**, the Metadata Service on **transactions per second**, and a 50 GB upload never ties up the service that answers "list this folder".

slides.title: Upload only what's missing: the Block Index
script: Here's how a commit avoids moving bytes. We keep a **Block Index**: a big key-value table from **hash to storage location**, with a reference count.

slides.title: Commit, upload what's missing, commit again
script: The client commits first, optimistically, with just the list of hashes. The Metadata Service checks the index and answers: "I'm **missing** these three blocks." The client uploads only those three to the Block Service, which records them in the index, and then retries the commit, which now succeeds. An edit to one slide of a big deck uploads one 4 MB block.

slides.title: Dedupe for free
script: The same check gives us **dedupe for free**. If anyone has ever uploaded those exact bytes, we already have the block, so a popular installer or a forwarded video gets stored once.

items.text: Same bytes → same hash → **one stored block**
items.detail: no matter who uploaded it, or how many times

items.text: A popular installer is stored once
items.detail: not once per user who downloaded it

items.text: A forwarded video is stored once
items.detail: every copy is a list of the same hashes

slides.title: Don't leak what others store
script: One caution: if we tell a client "we already have this block" for a block someone *else* uploaded, we leak whether a file exists in Dropbox. So we only skip the upload when the block is already in **one of this user's own files**, and dedupe across users quietly, on the server side.

columns: Skip the upload when the block is…
rows: yes: a probe for any file's contents
in someone else's (dedupe on the server)

slides.title: The client is half the system
script: Let's look at the client, because in Dropbox **the client is half the system**. Its **sync engine** watches the folder using OS file-system events, hashes changed files into blocks, and runs the commit protocol we just saw.

slides.title: The local index
script: It keeps a **local index**, a small SQLite database recording, for every file, the path, the block hashes and the server version it last synced. That's how it knows what changed while it was closed: on startup it compares the folder on disk against the local index, and only rehashes files whose size or modification time moved.

slides.title: The user's machine does the heavy lifting
script: The client also does the expensive work for us: **hashing, chunking and compression happen on the user's machine**, which spreads that CPU over hundreds of millions of devices instead of our data centers. And it's why a short outage on our side doesn't hurt much: the user's files are all still right there.

items.detail: CPU spread over hundreds of millions of devices

items.text: Our servers only check, store and serve
items.detail: no per-byte work in our data centers

items.text: **Outages are soft**: the files are still local
items.detail: sync pauses, the user keeps working

slides.title: The metadata is a journal
script: Now, how do other devices find out what changed? Rather than a table of current state that clients have to diff, we model the metadata as an **append-only journal**.

slides.title: Journal entries, ordered per namespace
script: Every change, whether an edit, a rename or a delete, is appended as a journal entry with a **monotonically increasing ID**. The scope of ordering is a **namespace**: a user's home folder is one namespace, and as we'll see, each shared folder is another. Within a namespace, every change has a strict order.

slides.title: Syncing from a cursor
script: Each device remembers a **cursor**, the last journal ID it applied. Syncing is then trivial: "give me everything in this namespace after cursor 81,442". A device that was offline for a week just asks for a longer list. Every device replays the **same changes in the same order**, which is exactly the convergence guarantee we asked for.

steps.note: offline for a week? just a longer list

slides.title: Telling devices something changed
script: Devices could poll the journal every few seconds, but 100 million devices polling would be a lot of load, almost all of it answering "nothing new". Instead, each device holds a **long-poll** connection to a **Notification Service**: "tell me when anything after my cursor shows up in my namespaces."

slides.title: Long poll, then list_changes
script: When a commit lands, the Metadata Service pings the Notification Service that the namespace changed, and the waiting connections return immediately. The device then calls **list_changes** on the Metadata Service to fetch the actual entries.

steps.note: connection held open, up to ~90 s

slides.title: A nudge, not a message
script: Notice the notification **carries no data**, it's just a nudge. That keeps it cheap and makes it safe to lose: if a ping is dropped, the device's long poll times out after about 90 seconds, it checks anyway, and catches up from its cursor. Correctness lives in the journal; notifications are only for speed.

items.detail: tiny, cheap to fan out

items.text: **Safe to lose**: the long poll times out at ~90 s
items.detail: the device checks anyway and catches up from its cursor
notifications are only for speed

slides.title: Why long-poll
script: Long-poll is plain HTTP, which works through corporate proxies better than WebSockets, and holding 100 million mostly idle connections is a job for a small fleet of event-driven servers.

rows: plain HTTP, proxy-friendly; idle connections are cheap

slides.title: A second device: the download path
script: Now add the user's **phone or a web browser**. Let's follow an edit made on the laptop to the phone.

slides.title: From the laptop to the phone
script: The laptop uploads its missing blocks and commits. The journal gets a new entry, the Notification Service wakes the phone's long poll, and the phone calls list_changes and learns "report.pdf is now blocks A, B and C". It compares that with what it has locally and **downloads only the blocks it doesn't already have**, by hash, straight from the Block Service.

slides.title: Eager metadata, lazy bytes
script: Phones and web clients don't keep a full copy of the folder; they **sync the metadata eagerly and the bytes lazily**, downloading a file only when the user opens it. Dropbox's desktop client can do the same with placeholder files. The tree is cheap, so every device has all of it; the bytes are expensive, so each device fetches only what it needs.

rows: lazily, when a file is opened

slides.title: Offline edits and conflicts
script: Now the hard case: the laptop is on a plane and edits **report.docx**, while the phone edits the same file. Both started from version 7.

slides.title: Optimistic concurrency
script: Every commit says which version it's based on: "make this file these blocks, **if it's still version 7**". The phone commits first and wins, creating version 8. When the laptop lands and commits on top of version 7, the Metadata Service rejects it, because the base is stale. That's **optimistic concurrency**, a conditional write on the journal.

steps.note: both edits start from report.docx v7

slides.title: The conflicted copy
script: The laptop can't merge two Word files, and we promised never to silently drop an edit. So the client pulls version 8, and saves its own edit as **"report (Sam's conflicted copy).docx"** right next to it, and commits that as a new file. The user sees both and decides. It's not elegant, but it's **simple, predictable and never loses data**, which is the right trade-off for arbitrary binary files.

steps.label: save own edit as "report (Sam's conflicted copy).docx"

steps.note: both files side by side; the user decides

slides.title: Shared folders are namespaces
script: Now sharing. When a user shares a folder, we **turn that folder into its own namespace**, with its own journal, and record who the members are and whether they can edit or only view.

slides.title: Members and mount points
script: Each member's home namespace gets a **mount point**: "namespace 77 appears at /Team Projects". A teammate's client subscribes to their home namespace *and* to every shared namespace mounted in it, each with its own cursor.

slides.title: One append, every member
script: An edit in the shared folder is one append to one journal, and every member's devices pick it up through exactly the same long-poll and list_changes path.
This is why the namespace is the unit of ordering: it's the **unit of sharing**.

slides.title: Permissions, and joining for free
script: Permission checks happen in the Metadata Service on every commit and every list, against the namespace's member list. And because blocks are content-addressed, a teammate joining a folder with 50 GB in it doesn't copy anything on our side; they just get access to hashes we already store.

items.text: **Every commit and every list** checks the members
items.detail: in the Metadata Service, per namespace

items.text: View-only members can list, but not commit
items.detail: the role lives on the member row
the new member just gets access to hashes we store

slides.title: Shard the metadata by namespace
script: One MySQL database won't hold a trillion file entries and 70,000 commits a second at peak. We **shard the metadata**, and the namespace makes the shard key obvious: **shard by namespace ID**.

slides.title: A namespace lives on one shard
script: Everything that needs to be ordered or transactional, a namespace's journal, its file rows, its cursors, lives on **one shard**, so a commit is a single-shard transaction and the journal ID is just an auto-increment on that shard. Nothing ever needs a cross-shard transaction to stay correct.

items.text: Journal, file rows, members: **one shard per namespace**
items.detail: everything ordered or transactional, together
no two-phase commit, ever

items.text: The journal ID is an **auto-increment** on that shard
items.detail: strict order for free

slides.title: Logical shards, physical clusters
script: We'd use many logical shards mapped onto fewer physical MySQL clusters, each with a primary and replicas, so we can move hot namespaces around. The awkward case is a **huge shared namespace**, a whole company's shared drive with millions of files; it can't be split across shards, so it gets a dedicated cluster. That's the trade-off for clean per-namespace ordering, and I think it's the right one.

rows: ns 5 · a company drive, millions of files

slides.title: A cache in front of the metadata
script: Reads vastly outnumber writes on the metadata side: every list_changes call, every folder listing on the web, every permission check, and every "which of these blocks are missing" lookup.
So we put a **cache tier**, memcache, in front of both the metadata shards and the Block Index.

slides.title: What goes in the cache
script: Block Index entries are perfect cache material, because a hash's location never changes. Namespace membership and folder listings are cached too, and **invalidated on commit**.

slides.title: Reads from cache, commits to the primary
script: The rule I'd keep is that the cache is only for **reads that can tolerate staleness**. The commit itself, the conditional "if it's still version 7" write, always goes to the shard's primary. A stale cache can make a device sync a moment late, but it can never make two devices disagree about the journal.

steps.note: stale cache → a late sync, never a disagreement

slides.title: A change log for everything downstream
script: Right now the Metadata Service pings the Notification Service directly. That's fragile: if the ping fails after the commit, devices wait for their poll timeout. And notifications aren't the only thing that cares about commits: version cleanup, search indexing, thumbnails, audit logs and analytics all want the same stream.

slides.title: Publish from the commit log
script: So every committed journal entry is also published to a **change log**, a Kafka topic **keyed by namespace**. Publishing comes from the database's own commit log, so an event exists **if and only if** the commit happened. Keying by namespace keeps each namespace's events in order within a partition.

steps.label: from the DB's commit log, key = ns 12

steps.note: event exists if and only if the commit happened

slides.title: One log, many consumers
script: The Notification Service is now just one consumer. Each feature I put out of scope, like search or previews, would be another consumer of this same log. That's where it plugs in, without adding work to the commit path.

items.detail: the first consumer
next slide
out of scope, but this is where they plug in
no extra work on the commit path

slides.title: Version history and garbage collection
script: Version history mostly falls out of the design already. A file version is a journal entry pointing at a list of hashes, and **blocks are immutable**, so keeping old versions costs a few hundred bytes of metadata plus whatever blocks changed.

slides.title: Restores and deletes are just commits
script: **Restoring** version 3 is just a new commit pointing at version 3's hashes; no bytes move.
Deletes work the same way: a delete is a journal entry, and the file's blocks stay put for the 30-day window.

slides.title: The GC worker
script: What we need is a **GC worker**. It consumes the change log, and when a version ages past the retention window it **decrements the reference counts** of its blocks in the Block Index. When a block's count reaches zero, it's deleted from storage.

steps.note: A and C are still referenced by v5

slides.title: Slow and paranoid
script: GC is where data loss bugs hide, so I'd make it deliberately slow and paranoid: mark blocks first, wait days, re-verify that nothing references them, and only then delete. Leaking some storage is cheap; deleting a live block is unforgivable.

items.detail: don't delete anything yet
let in-flight commits and lagging consumers catch up
scan, don't trust the counter alone
leaked storage is cheap; a deleted live block is not

slides.title: Share links and the CDN
script: Now **share links**. A link is a random, unguessable token that maps to a file or folder at a path, plus settings like expiry or a password. Resolving it is a cheap metadata lookup.

slides.title: Resolve, redirect, serve from the edge
script: The bytes are the interesting part. A link posted on social media can be downloaded by a million strangers in an hour, and we don't want that traffic hammering the Block Service. So link downloads go through a **CDN**.

When a visitor clicks, we resolve the link, check it's still valid, and redirect them to a short-lived, **signed CDN URL**; the CDN fetches from the Block Service once and serves everyone else from the edge.

steps.note: everyone after that is served from the edge

slides.title: Cached forever
script: Content addressing makes this unusually easy: a block never changes, so it can be **cached forever** with no invalidation. If the owner edits the file, the link resolves to new hashes, and therefore new cache keys.

items.detail: so the CDN can cache it forever
the hardest part of CDN caching disappears

items.text: An edit means **new hashes, new cache keys**
items.detail: the link resolves to the new version

slides.title: Eleven nines: erasure coding and regions
script: Durability lives in **Block Storage**. At exabyte scale, I'd seriously consider **building our own** storage layer instead of renting S3, as Dropbox did with Magic Pocket; at this size, it's cheaper.

slides.title: Erasure coding instead of three copies
script: Inside a region, instead of keeping three full copies, we use **erasure coding**: split a group of blocks into, say, 8 data fragments plus 4 parity fragments, spread across racks and zones. Any 8 of the 12 can rebuild the data, so we survive several simultaneous disk or rack failures with about **1.5× overhead instead of 3×**. On 3 exabytes, that difference is billions of dollars in hardware.

slides.title: Other regions and scrubbers
script: And every block is **replicated asynchronously to another region**, so losing an entire data center loses nothing. Background **scrubbers** constantly re-read blocks and verify them against their hashes, which content addressing gives us for free, and repair anything that's rotted before a second failure finds it.

items.detail: losing a whole data center loses nothing

items.text: **Scrubbers** re-read every block, all the time
items.detail: and check it against its hash, for free
before a second failure finds it

slides.title: Cold storage for cold blocks
script: Storage is our biggest cost, and most of it is **cold**: old photos, finished projects, files nobody has opened in a year. Access follows a steep curve, with most reads hitting recently written data.

slides.title: Hot tier vs cold tier
script: So blocks that haven't been read in a while **age out to a cold tier**: denser disks, wider erasure codes with less overhead, and fewer replicas in hot regions. Reads from the cold tier are a bit slower, a few hundred milliseconds more, which is fine for a file nobody has touched since 2019.

rows: blocks not read in a while

slides.title: Moving a block is invisible
script: Because blocks are addressed by hash, moving one between tiers is invisible to everything above: only its location in the Block Index changes. None of the metadata, the journal, the clients or the links ever notice.

steps.label: copy block h7 (unread for a year)

steps.note: journal, clients and links still just say "h7"

slides.title: Metadata across regions
script: The last piece is the **metadata across regions**. Block replication alone isn't enough: if a region goes down, we also need the file tree to keep working.

slides.title: Primary, replica, failover
script: Each metadata shard has a **primary in one region** and replicas in another, kept up to date by MySQL replication. Writes for a namespace always go to its primary, which preserves the single order per namespace that the whole design depends on. If a region fails, we **promote the replicas** in the other region. We might lose the last second or so of commits, but the clients still hold those changes locally and will simply commit them again.

steps.note: region A fails; the last ~1 s never arrived

slides.title: Why not multi-master
script: I would **not** make the metadata multi-master. Two regions both accepting commits to the same namespace would break the ordering guarantee, and we'd be back to resolving conflicts on the server. A short failover is a much better trade-off for four nines.

rows: no failover, but conflicts on the server

slides.title: The complete system
script: Let's step back and look at the whole thing. Everything is organized around one split: the **file bytes** and the **file tree**.

The **bytes** are content-addressed 4 MB blocks: hashed on the client, uploaded only when missing, deduplicated, stored with erasure coding, aged into cold storage, replicated across regions and cached forever at the CDN. They're immutable, so all of that is simple.

The **tree** is a journal per namespace in sharded MySQL. One shard per namespace gives us strictly ordered commits, optimistic concurrency for conflicts, and cursors that let any device catch up after a minute or a month. A change log fans every commit out to notifications and garbage collection.

And the **client** does half the work: it watches, hashes and keeps a local index, so sync is incremental, survives outages and never loses an edit. If I had more time, I'd go deeper on the sync engine's edge cases, like case-insensitive file systems and moves across shared folders, or on LAN sync between devices in the same office. But this is the shape of Dropbox.
